name: Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model
what: This subtopic covers Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping as a psychological model of stress, focusing on primary appraisal (including benign-positive, irrelevant, and stressful appraisals with harm/loss, threat, and challenge sub-appraisals) and secondary appraisal (including emotion-focused and problem-focused coping strategies). It also covers the model's strengths and limitations.
why: This is the key psychological model of stress in the study design and provides the counterpart to Selye's biological model. Understanding it allows students to explain individual differences in stress responses and apply both models to the same scenario.

items.title: I can explain what makes Lazarus and Folkman's model a psychological and transactional model of stress
items.what: The model is psychological because it focuses on subjective cognitive and affective appraisals of stressors rather than biological responses. It is transactional because stress is the output resulting from a transaction between an incoming stressor and the individual's personal appraisal of it and their available coping resources.
items.why: Understanding why this model is described as psychological and transactional is required for comparison questions with Selye's GAS and for correctly framing exam answers.
items.example: Two students receive the same exam result. One appraises it as a threat to their future (producing distress), while another appraises it as a challenge to improve (producing eustress). The stress that results is a product of this subjective transaction, not the result alone.

items.title: I can describe the first substage of primary appraisal, including the three possible initial appraisals
items.what: In the first substage of primary appraisal, the individual evaluates whether an incoming stimulus will cause them stress. The three possible appraisals are: irrelevant (not an issue for the individual), benign-positive (neutral or good, not stressful), or stressful (a source of worry or emotional significance). Only a stressful appraisal continues the transaction.
items.why: Students must know all three initial appraisals and understand that the model only progresses if the stimulus is judged stressful. This is frequently tested using novel scenarios.
items.example: A student hears that a new elective subject has been added to the school timetable. They appraise it as irrelevant because it does not affect them. No further appraisal occurs and no stress results.

items.title: I can describe the second substage of primary appraisal, including harm/loss, threat, and challenge
items.what: If the stimulus is appraised as stressful, the individual further categorises the nature of that stress: harm/loss means the stressor has already caused damage; threat means the stressor may cause damage in the future; challenge means the stressor may offer a positive opportunity for growth or change.
items.why: All three sub-appraisals produce different emotional responses and lead to different coping behaviours in secondary appraisal. Exam questions regularly ask students to identify which sub-appraisal applies to a given scenario and justify their answer.
items.example: Thomas is anxious about learning to drive. He appraises it as a threat because he fears future accidents and financial strain, not because anything bad has happened yet.

items.title: I can describe secondary appraisal and the two types of coping strategies it involves
items.what: Secondary appraisal is the evaluation of what coping resources are required and whether they are available. If coping resources are judged adequate, stress is reduced or eliminated. If inadequate, stress continues. Two coping strategies are identified: problem-focused coping (directly targeting the source of the stressor) and emotion-focused coping (targeting the emotional components of the stressor indirectly).
items.why: Secondary appraisal explains why two people who make the same primary appraisal of a stressor can still end up with different stress levels. It is also directly linked to the coping strategies content in lesson 3E.
items.example: Yasmin appraises running out of savings as a threat (primary appraisal) and then evaluates whether she has enough time and income opportunities to rebuild them (secondary appraisal). Concluding she does not, her stress increases.

items.title: I can give examples of problem-focused and emotion-focused coping strategies
items.what: Problem-focused strategies directly address the source of the stressor: making a plan, seeking information, taking action, time management. Emotion-focused strategies address the emotional experience of the stressor indirectly: wishful thinking, denial, reframing, venting, meditation, distraction.
items.why: Students must be able to identify and apply both types of coping strategy to novel scenarios. Neither type is inherently superior; effectiveness depends on the specific context of the stressor.
items.example: A student stressed about an upcoming SAC uses problem-focused coping by making a study timetable, and emotion-focused coping by calling a friend to vent before returning to study.

items.title: I can evaluate the explanatory power of Lazarus and Folkman's model by identifying its strengths and limitations
items.what: Strengths: the model accounts for individual differences in stress responses, uses human subjects, incorporates cognitive processes, and provides coping strategies. Limitations: primary and secondary appraisal may occur simultaneously rather than in sequence, individuals are not always consciously aware of their appraisals, and the model lacks empirical support because internal appraisal processes are difficult to test.
items.why: Evaluating both models and comparing them is explicitly required by the study design. What is typically a strength of the Lazarus and Folkman model is often a limitation of Selye's GAS, and vice versa.
items.example: A strength: the model explains why Dean is less stressed than Yasmin after the same trip, because their appraisals differ. A limitation: neither Dean nor Yasmin may be consciously aware of the appraisal steps the model describes.
